gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the $1,365 Solis S6 5 kW 'hybrid' (S6-EH1P5K-H-US) accepts only high-voltage lithium batteries in a 120–500 V window. The common 48 V (51.2 V) rack or wall batteries that every other hybrid in the answer and the rival pages uses sit far below that window, so the Solis cannot run on them.
standout_why: I checked three pages. ecosolarkits.com/blogs/guides/hybrid-vs-off-grid-vs-grid-tie-inverter covers anti-islanding shutdown (UL 1741 / IEEE 1547) and when you need 120/240 V split phase, but it never says whether a given inverter takes a high-voltage or a 48 V battery. liveoffthegrid.com/specs/inverters lists only 48 V hybrids and says 'battery voltage constrains the whole system' but has no high-voltage hybrids and no warning about mixing them. homebackupco.com's Rich Solar page gives only that unit's 24 V battery and 120 V output. None of the three mentions the Solis S6-H-US or its 120–500 V battery window. Rivals already cover grid-tie shutdown and the 120 V vs 240 V issue, so those findings would not stand out.
decides: This is a cost trap, not a dead end. ChatGPT's cheapest 'hybrid, solar + battery storage' card, the Solis S6 5 kW, works only with high-voltage stacks from Solis's compatibility list (BYD HVL, Dyness Tower, Soluna HV and similar), not with a 48 V battery. A shopper with a $3,000 budget who means 'inverter plus a cheap battery' should pick a 48 V hybrid such as the Rich Solar 3K 48 V or Sol-Ark 5K, or plan for a high-voltage battery. The SMA Sunny Boy has no battery port at all. SMA's own manual says its outage outlet works only in daylight and never at night.
